title: Synonyms and Antonyms: Choosing by Context

blocks.text: "She looked slim in that dress." "She looked skinny in that dress." A dictionary lists the two words as synonyms, yet one is a compliment and the other is not. Synonym questions are never about matching definitions — they are about matching the sentence you were given.

blocks.markdown:
A **synonym** is a word with nearly the same meaning as another. An **antonym** is a word with the opposite meaning.

Notice the word *nearly*. English has very few exact synonyms, because words differ in three ways beyond their basic sense:

- **Connotation** — the feeling attached: *slim* approves, *skinny* criticises.
- **Register** — how formal it is: *purchase* in a contract, *buy* in conversation.
- **Collocation** — the company it keeps: *heavy rain* but *strong tea*, never the reverse.

blocks.title: Connotation
blocks.text: The attitude or emotional colouring a word carries in addition to its plain meaning. *Thrifty*, *economical* and *stingy* all describe someone who does not spend much, but the first praises, the second is neutral and the third condemns.

blocks.title: Using context when a word has two meanings
blocks.prompt: Choose the meaning of the bold word: "The guards on duty at the gate were **relieved** at six o'clock in the morning."

steps.text: List the possible senses of the word. *Relieve* can mean to ease somebody's distress, or to take over somebody's duty.
Do not settle for the commoner sense. Look instead for clues in the sentence.
Note the clue words: *on duty*, *at the gate*, *at six o'clock in the morning*. These belong to the language of shifts and rosters.
Test the first sense against the clues. Nothing in the sentence says the guards were suffering, so there is no distress to ease.
Test the second sense. A precise time plus a reference to duty fits a handover perfectly.
Choose the duty sense: the guards were replaced by others coming on shift.

blocks.answer: Replaced by others — the reference to duty and a precise hour points to a change of shift, not to comfort

items: Read the whole sentence, not only the bold word — the context is part of the question.
Decide the part of speech first; a synonym must belong to the same word class.
Check whether the question asks for the nearest meaning or the opposite. Rushing this is the commonest cause of lost marks.
Eliminate options that are synonyms when an antonym is wanted; examiners always plant one.
Test the surviving options by substituting each into the original sentence.
Prefer the option whose connotation matches the tone of the sentence.

blocks.title: The planted synonym
blocks.text: In an antonym question, one option is almost always a synonym of the target word. In question after question candidates who read only the bold word choose it. Underline the words *opposite in meaning* in the rubric before you look at the options.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Build vocabulary from reading rather than from word lists. When you meet a new word in a newspaper, write the whole sentence in your notebook, not just the word. You will then remember its connotation and the words it keeps company with, which is what the exam actually tests.

points: Synonyms share a core meaning but differ in connotation, register and collocation.
Very few English synonyms are interchangeable in every sentence.
The context of the sentence, not the commonest dictionary sense, decides the answer.
Match the part of speech before comparing meanings.
In antonym questions, expect a synonym to be planted among the options.
Learn new words inside whole sentences so that you learn their feel as well as their meaning.
